scenes.heading: Green chemistry principles
scenes.sub: Stop waste at the design stage, not afterwards
scenes.say: Chemistry gives us medicines, fuels and materials, but it has often made toxic waste too. Green chemistry asks: what if we designed the problem out from the start?

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: Cutting biscuits from dough leaves offcuts
scenes.science: Atom economy: how much of the reactants ends up as product
scenes.breaks: you can re-roll dough offcuts, but by-product atoms usually can't go back in. And atom economy is worked out on paper.
scenes.say: When you cut round biscuits out of dough, there are offcuts left over. Atom economy asks, before you start, how much of the dough is designed to end up as biscuits. The biscuits are the desired product, and the offcuts are by-products. Square biscuits leave no offcuts, like an addition reaction with one hundred percent atom economy.

The biscuits are the desired product, and the offcuts are by-products. Square biscuits leave no offcuts, like an addition reaction with 100% atom economy.

scenes.heading: Two kinds of economy

right.title: Circular
points: e.g. cans remelted into new cans

scenes.say: A linear economy is a line to the bin: take, make, use, throw away. A circular economy is a loop back to the factory. Products are reused, repaired and recycled, like aluminium cans being remelted into new cans.

scenes.heading: Some of the 12 principles
points: Prevention: avoid waste, don't clean up
scenes.say: There are twelve principles. The first is prevention: it's better not to make waste than to clean it up. Others include high atom economy, safer solvents like water, renewable feedstocks like plants, and catalysts that allow milder conditions.

scenes.heading: Atom economy
scenes.say: Atom economy equals the molar mass of the desired product, divided by the molar mass of all the reactants, times one hundred. Always use the coefficients from the balanced equation.

scenes.heading: Worked example
scenes.question: Find the atom economy for making ethanol by fermentation: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂
scenes.say: Fermenting glucose gives two ethanol molecules, ninety-two grams per mole in total, from one glucose at one hundred and eighty. Ninety-two over one eighty, times one hundred, is fifty-one point one percent. Making ethanol from ethene scores one hundred percent, but uses crude oil. So you weigh several principles.
scenes.caption: Fermenting glucose gives two ethanol, 92.0 g mol⁻¹ in total, from one glucose at 180.0. 92.0 ÷ 180.0 × 100 = 51.1%. Making ethanol from ethene is 100%, but it uses crude oil. So being green means weighing several principles.

scenes.heading: Don't mix these up

right.title: Percentage yield
points: What you got vs what you could get

scenes.say: Don't confuse atom economy with yield. Atom economy is worked out on paper from the equation. Yield compares what you actually got with what you could have got. A perfect yield can still have a poor atom economy.

points: Green chemistry prevents waste by design
Circular economy keeps materials in use
scenes.say: Quick recap. Green chemistry prevents waste at the design stage. A circular economy keeps materials in use. Atom economy is product over all reactants, times one hundred. And judging what's greenest means weighing several principles. Now try the practice questions!
